# 135 · A window counter with the previous count proved equal on the start and the count

[← All examples](../README.md)

| Verdict | Categories | Severity if shipped | Change | Verified unit | Approach |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **✓ Verified: equivalent on every input** | functional, no-false-positive | none | feature, behaviour change intended | [`Window#counted`](../../examples/apps/crosscut/src/main/java/net/terminalvalue/crosscut/ratelimit/Window.java) | [B9: Regression verification](../../lib/README.md) |

> The same change to Crosscut's `Window` record done right: the counter gains a `previousCount` component and an `estimated` method, and `counted` keeps the alignment of the start to the clock, `nowNanos - nowNanos % windowNanos`, carrying the count only into the window right after the one it was in. The regression proof relates the new record result to the old one on the two components they share, with the old counter built from the new components, and proves the start and the count equal on every input, the tool's own checker in seconds.

Tags: [resilience](../README.md#tag-resilience), [clocks-and-time](../README.md#tag-clocks-and-time), [confined-change](../README.md#tag-confined-change), [record-components](../README.md#tag-record-components), [signature-change](../README.md#tag-signature-change), [own-checker](../README.md#tag-own-checker)

## The change

Add a `previousCount` component to the record and an `estimated(nowNanos, windowNanos)` method that weights it by how much of the previous window the sliding window still covers. `counted` keeps computing the window's start from the clock, `nowNanos - nowNanos % windowNanos`, and when the request opens a new window its previous count is this window's count if that window ended where the new one starts, zero otherwise. The tests take the third component, and one is added for the estimate.

The record the method belongs to changed, so the developer states how the previous version's receiver is built from the new parameters, and how it is called: `Window#counted(nowNanos, windowNanos)` on `new Window(this.startNanos, this.count)`. The verifier proves that on every input, the new method agrees with the previous one called that way, or shows one on which it does not.

The result changed its type or its meaning, so the developer states how the two results are related, `previous` being the result of `Window#counted` and `result` the new method's: `previous.startNanos == result.startNanos && previous.count == result.count`. The verifier proves that the relation holds on every input where both versions return, and that they throw alike where they throw, or shows an input on which they do not.

**Before** ([`Window.java`](../../examples/apps/crosscut/src/main/java/net/terminalvalue/crosscut/ratelimit/Window.java), line 1):

```java
package net.terminalvalue.crosscut.ratelimit;

/**
 * A fixed-window request counter, the simplest rate limit: how many requests a client has made in the window its
 * last request fell in, with windows of one length aligned to the epoch (Spring Cloud Gateway's rate limiter keeps
 * such a count per key and window; Resilience4j's {@code RateLimiter} calls the window a cycle). The counter is a
 * value: the filter keeps one per client, replaces it on each request with what {@link #counted} returns, and
 * refuses the request when the count passes the limit. The clock reading and the window length are arguments, so
 * that the counter is a pure function.
 *
 * <p>A counter starts as {@code new Window(0, 0)}: no request yet, in the window at the epoch.
 */
public record Window(long startNanos, long count) {

    public Window {
        if (startNanos < 0 || count < 0) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("the start and the count must not be negative");
        }
    }

    /**
     * The counter after a request at {@code nowNanos}, with windows of {@code windowNanos}: one more in the same
     * window, or the first request of the window the reading falls in.
     */
    public Window counted(long nowNanos, long windowNanos) {
        if (windowNanos <= 0 || nowNanos < startNanos) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("the window must be positive and time must not go back");
        }
        long start = nowNanos - nowNanos % windowNanos;
        return start == startNanos ? new Window(startNanos, count + 1) : new Window(start, 1);
    }
}
```

**After:**

```java
package net.terminalvalue.crosscut.ratelimit;

/**
 * A sliding-window request counter, the rate limit that does not let a client spend two limits at a window
 * boundary: how many requests a client has made in the window its last request fell in, and how many in the window
 * before it, with windows of one length aligned to the epoch (Spring Cloud Gateway's rate limiter keeps such a
 * count per key and window; Resilience4j's {@code RateLimiter} calls the window a cycle). The counter is a value:
 * the filter keeps one per client, replaces it on each request with what {@link #counted} returns, and refuses the
 * request when {@link #estimated} passes the limit. The clock reading and the window length are arguments, so that
 * the counter is a pure function.
 *
 * <p>A counter starts as {@code new Window(0, 0, 0)}: no request yet, in the window at the epoch.
 */
public record Window(long startNanos, long count, long previousCount) {

    public Window {
        if (startNanos < 0 || count < 0 || previousCount < 0) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("the start and the counts must not be negative");
        }
    }

    /**
     * The counter after a request at {@code nowNanos}, with windows of {@code windowNanos}: one more in the same
     * window, or the first request of the window the reading falls in, with the count of the window just before
     * it, if that is the one this counter was in, as the previous count.
     */
    public Window counted(long nowNanos, long windowNanos) {
        if (windowNanos <= 0 || nowNanos < startNanos) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("the window must be positive and time must not go back");
        }
        long start = nowNanos - nowNanos % windowNanos;
        if (start == startNanos) {
            return new Window(startNanos, count + 1, previousCount);
        }
        return new Window(start, 1, start - startNanos == windowNanos ? count : 0);
    }

    /**
     * The requests in the window of {@code windowNanos} ending at {@code nowNanos}, estimated as the current
     * window's count plus the previous window's count weighted by how much of that sliding window it covers
     * (the approximation Cloudflare's rate limiter uses).
     */
    public long estimated(long nowNanos, long windowNanos) {
        if (windowNanos <= 0 || nowNanos < startNanos) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("the window must be positive and time must not go back");
        }
        long elapsed = Math.min(windowNanos, nowNanos - startNanos);
        return count + previousCount * (windowNanos - elapsed) / windowNanos;
    }
}
```

## What the verifier found

For every input, the new code returns a result related to the old code's by `previous.startNanos == result.startNanos && previous.count == result.count`, or throws what it threw, the old code being called with the arguments `new Window(this.startNanos, this.count), nowNanos, windowNanos` computed from the new parameters.

This is a proof over the whole domain (this: Window(startNanos: long, count: long, previousCount: long) × nowNanos: long × windowNanos: long), not a sample. The tool's own checker ran the harness symbolically, path by path, with its bundled SAT solver deciding at each branch which sides are feasible, and no feasible path reaches the assertion: no input exists on which they differ.

## Would the existing tests have caught it?

Every existing unit test passes, as it should (`java -ea net.terminalvalue.crosscut.Tests`, run against the patched code).

## Why it matters

None: the proof is over every counter, clock reading and window length, the start and the count unchanged. What is at stake is the review of a method that returns a record of other components than before: a reviewer has to see that the two components the filter's limit depends on are computed as they were, and the proof is that.

## Why the verdict is right

The harness takes the three components, the clock reading and the window length as symbolic inputs, builds the new record from them and the old one from the start and the count, skips what either constructor rejects, calls both versions, and reads the components of the two result records into the relation, which must hold whenever both return (two null records would agree, one alone would not, and neither version returns null). Both versions compute the start as `nowNanos - nowNanos % windowNanos` and the count as one more or one, and throw for the same inputs; the previous count the new record carries is outside the relation. The tool's own checker proves it in seconds, the two 64-bit remainders being one circuit; JBMC did not finish within a minute on the same harness.

## What to do

Merge. The proof is the review of the two components the limit depends on; the new component is reviewed by its tests and its own property, if one is written.

## Notes

- No scope: the relation holds on every input, including an unaligned start and time or window values the methods refuse, since both versions throw for the same inputs (a non-positive window, a reading before the start, a count that overflows into the constructor's check) and the start and the count are computed the same way. The checker proves it without a scope, where 134 needs one to show the telling witness.
- The relation names the components the two records share, `previous.startNanos == result.startNanos && previous.count == result.count`; `result.previousCount` is a name it could use, `previous.previousCount` is not, and the tool says so. Without a relation the tool refuses with `the result's components changed: Window(startNanos: long, count: long) before, Window(startNanos: long, count: long, previousCount: long) now` and proposes this very expression, the equalities of the components the records share by name and type.
- Both versions compute `nowNanos % windowNanos` on the same inputs, so in the tool's own checker the two 64-bit remainders are one circuit (as 120's divisions are, see its notes), and the proof is 9 paths and 10 solver calls. When this example was written it still took about 12 s, nearly all of it in CaDiCaL proving the paths infeasible with the remainder's circuit in them (the release build is no faster than the debug one: the time is the solver's). Since then the checker leaves a division to the solver as bits under what holds of every division (the remainder is smaller than the divisor and takes the dividend's sign, a division by one is exact, a power of two divides by masking) and builds the circuit only where a model got it wrong: the same proof takes 0.3 s, 11 solver calls, the circuit built once, the facts being what the infeasibility of the paths rests on. JBMC, with its default solver, did not finish the same harness within 60 s, nor with its arithmetic refinement (`--refine-arithmetic`) within 90 s, which is why the example names the checker (`approach.engine`: native).
- The statement the harness prints reads the relation as Java, `previous.startNanos() == result.startNanos() && previous.count() == result.count()`, with `before.net.terminalvalue.crosscut.ratelimit.Window previous = a; net.terminalvalue.crosscut.ratelimit.Window result = b;` before it.

## Evidence

How the verdict was reached: jvmcontract's own checker (CaDiCaL): 1 properties proved over this: Window(startNanos: long, count: long, previousCount: long) × nowNanos: long × windowNanos: long in 0.1 s; loops unwound 16 times with unwinding assertions.

/** Generated by jvmcontract: asserts that two versions of a method agree. The class file JBMC checks is generated directly; this is the same statement, for readers. */
public final class EquivalenceHarness {
    public static void check(long this_startNanos, long this_count, long this_previousCount, long nowNanos, long windowNanos) {
        // The records, from their components, in both versions; an input a constructor rejects is outside the statement.
        net.terminalvalue.crosscut.ratelimit.Window this_after; // the previous version takes the components
        try { this_after = new net.terminalvalue.crosscut.ratelimit.Window(this_startNanos, this_count, this_previousCount); } catch (Throwable t) { return; }
        // The previous version's arguments, from the new parameters; an input for which one throws (a record its constructor rejects) is outside the relation.
        before.net.terminalvalue.crosscut.ratelimit.Window this_ = new before.net.terminalvalue.crosscut.ratelimit.Window(this_startNanos, this_count); long nowNanos_ = nowNanos; long windowNanos_ = windowNanos;
        before.net.terminalvalue.crosscut.ratelimit.Window a = null;
        int ea = 0;
        try { a = this_.counted(nowNanos_, windowNanos_); } catch (java.lang.NumberFormatException t) { ea = 1; } catch (java.lang.ArithmeticException t) { ea = 2; } catch (java.lang.NullPointerException t) { ea = 3; } catch (java.lang.ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException t) { ea = 4; } catch (java.lang.StringIndexOutOfBoundsException t) { ea = 5; } catch (java.lang.IndexOutOfBoundsException t) { ea = 6; } catch (java.lang.NegativeArraySizeException t) { ea = 7; } catch (java.lang.ClassCastException t) { ea = 8; } catch (java.lang.IllegalStateException t) { ea = 9; } catch (java.lang.IllegalArgumentException t) { ea = 10; } catch (java.lang.UnsupportedOperationException t) { ea = 11; } catch (java.util.NoSuchElementException t) { ea = 12; } catch (java.util.ConcurrentModificationException t) { ea = 13; } catch (java.lang.RuntimeException t) { ea = 14; } catch (java.lang.Error t) { ea = 15; }
        net.terminalvalue.crosscut.ratelimit.Window b = null;
        int eb = 0;
        try { b = this_after.counted(nowNanos, windowNanos); } catch (java.lang.NumberFormatException t) { eb = 1; } catch (java.lang.ArithmeticException t) { eb = 2; } catch (java.lang.NullPointerException t) { eb = 3; } catch (java.lang.ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException t) { eb = 4; } catch (java.lang.StringIndexOutOfBoundsException t) { eb = 5; } catch (java.lang.IndexOutOfBoundsException t) { eb = 6; } catch (java.lang.NegativeArraySizeException t) { eb = 7; } catch (java.lang.ClassCastException t) { eb = 8; } catch (java.lang.IllegalStateException t) { eb = 9; } catch (java.lang.IllegalArgumentException t) { eb = 10; } catch (java.lang.UnsupportedOperationException t) { eb = 11; } catch (java.util.NoSuchElementException t) { eb = 12; } catch (java.util.ConcurrentModificationException t) { eb = 13; } catch (java.lang.RuntimeException t) { eb = 14; } catch (java.lang.Error t) { eb = 15; }
        // The results agree when the stated relation holds: previous is the previous version's, result the new one's (two null records agree, one alone does not).
        before.net.terminalvalue.crosscut.ratelimit.Window previous = a; net.terminalvalue.crosscut.ratelimit.Window result = b;
        assert ea == eb && (ea != 0 || (previous.startNanos() == result.startNanos() && previous.count() == result.count()));
    }
}
